comparison: Perfect agreement on experimental design and participant characteristics (C5, C6, C22, C23, C24). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers explicitly praising the rigorous methods, large sample size, and double-blind randomized design.

Perfect agreement on practice effects (C25, C26). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the statistical significance and methodological importance, while peer reviewers treated these as expected methodological observations without challenge.

Perfect agreement on drug manipulation checks (C27, C28). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights the significant Drug × Time interaction, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted these findings as evidence that subjective effects did not drive performance differences.

Divergent evaluations of primary behavioral findings (C30-C33, C7-C8, C75-C76). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to marginal significance (p=0.07), while peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, with the editor explicitly stating evidence is 'convincing' and claims are 'sufficiently qualified' despite the marginal interaction.

Perfect agreement on RT variability findings (C34-C37). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the statistical significance and effect sizes, while peer reviewers accepted these as supporting evidence for attention-related mechanisms without challenge.

Perfect agreement on learning dynamics and temporal specificity (C38-C42). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights the Bai-Perron breakpoint analysis and significant late learning effects, while peer reviewers confirmed MA improved learning in noisy blocks for low performers.

Perfect agreement on model validation (C43, C44). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the rigorous model comparison and simulation validation, while peer reviewers specifically requested and accepted simulation evidence that eta parameter changes drive performance improvements.

Perfect agreement on eta parameter findings (C45-C47, C59, C62, C69-C70). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights the significant reduction in eta and its specificity, while peer reviewers confirmed the enhancement reflects reduced dynamic up-regulation of learning rates in low performers.

Perfect agreement on learning rate dynamics (C48-C54). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the statistical significance of reduced variability and increased SNR, while peer reviewers explicitly described the pattern of volatile learning rates undermining performance.

Perfect agreement on behavioral validation of eta (C55-C57). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights the significant correlation and behavioral improvements, while peer reviewers accepted these as supporting the main narrative about learning from misleading feedback.

Perfect agreement on regression and simulation analyses (C58, C60-C61). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the coherent explanation for baseline-dependent effects, while peer reviewers specifically requested and accepted simulation evidence linking eta to performance.

Perfect agreement on parameter specificity (C63, C64). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights the selective effect on eta, while peer reviewers initially questioned why MA affected eta rather than inverse temperature but ultimately accepted this after revisions.

Slight divergence on exploratory simulations (C65-C68). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative and not fit to participant data. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED but did not explicitly discuss these analyses, suggesting implicit acceptance of appropriately qualified exploratory findings.

Agreement on methodological conclusions (C77-C80). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED, though OpenEval notes C78 is speculative. Peer reviewers accepted these as valid observations, with the editor noting claims are 'sufficiently qualified.' Both acknowledge these are secondary interpretations.

Perfect agreement on neurobiological mechanisms (C71-C74). Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes lack of direct measurement of neurotransmitters, while peer reviewers explicitly noted the limitation that methamphetamine affects multiple neuromodulatory systems, making it impossible to determine which is responsible.

Partial overlap on methodological recommendations (C80, C82). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED for both claims, while peer reviewers only explicitly addressed C80. Both agree on the successful control of practice effects and lack of session order effects.

Divergent evaluations of main conclusions (C85-C86, C9). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the 'causal link' claim is overstated given marginal behavioral effects (p=0.07). Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, with the editor stating evidence is 'convincing' and all reviewers accepting the core findings without challenge.

Divergent evaluations of double-blinding claim (C23). OpenEval rates experimental design including double-blinding as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewer R17 rates as UNCERTAIN, noting that participants' awareness of different drug experiences means blinding was effectively single-blind to experimenters only, not truly double-blind.

OpenEval evaluated background and literature review claims (C1-C4, C10-C11) as SUPPORTED with extensive citations establishing theoretical framework. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not explicitly assess background claims.

OpenEval evaluated comprehensive literature review (C12-C21) as SUPPORTED, noting accurate representation of prior work on catecholamines and individual differences. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not explicitly assess literature review claims.

OpenEval evaluated basic task validation (C29) as SUPPORTED based on visual inspection of choice probabilities tracking reward probabilities. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not explicitly discuss this basic validation.
